findings.title: Redirect-follow loop limit reduced 10x without justification
findings.body: The loop bound `for i = 0, 1000 do` was lowered from 10000. The original comment explicitly warned that this limit is the maximum depth of redirect chains that get joined; depths above it leave segment trees unjoined. Cutting the limit to 1000 means 10x more chains (especially long, deep spans trees common in distributed traces with many ancestor pointers) will silently fail to be merged, producing orphaned/incomplete segments flushed on the no-root timeout. The PR description ("Test 2") does not justify this regression.

findings.title: Eviction silently drops spans with no metric or log
findings.body: When `span_count > 1000` the script calls `zpopmin set_key, span_count - 1000`. Because the score is `end_timestamp_precise`, ZPOPMIN evicts the OLDEST ones in time. This is silent data loss: spans are permanently removed from the segment, no metric is incremented, no log is emitted, and the segment will be flushed incomplete with no way for operators to detect the loss. Even the prior Python-side metric `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` is no longer reachable (see buffer.py finding). At minimum, emit a `redis.call`/server-side metric (e.g. `INCR spans.buffer.add_buffer.evicted`) so this is observable.

findings.title: KeyError on messages missing `end_timestamp_precise`
findings.body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises KeyError if the field is absent. This field is not part of the original schema validated for `SpanEvent`, and any messages produced before this rollout (including in-flight backlog topics, retained Kafka segments, and relays that have not been updated) will crash the consumer's `process_batch` for every message. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (and consider how `0.0` interacts with zset ordering) or reject/log with a metric instead of hard-crashing.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative offset to Django queryset
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[cursor.offset:stop])`. Django querysets do NOT support negative slice starts (the QuerySet.__getitem__ implementation raises `AssertionError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`). The accompanying comment ("The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically") is factually wrong. Any cursor with a negative offset routed through this branch (which the audit-logs endpoint now creates whenever a superuser/global-access admin sends `optimized_pagination=true`) will produce a 500.

findings.title: Negative offset clamp only applied for non-prev cursors
findings.body: The defensive change is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For `cursor.is_prev=True` with a negative offset (still reachable through legitimate cursor strings), `offset` is used directly as a slice start and Django will still raise AssertionError. Either always clamp (`start_offset = max(0, offset)`) or validate at the Cursor layer.

findings.title: max_segment_spans check removed without replacement
findings.body: The previous loop had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` which deleted oversized segments and emitted a metric. This guard is removed; the Lua-side eviction (see add-buffer.lua finding) is the only cap on count. But eviction happens at insert time and is bounded at 1000, while `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001 — leaving no headroom and removing the only operator-visible signal. Either restore the check or delete the dead constructor parameter and update the docstring.

findings.title: max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now unused
findings.body: `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` is still accepted by `SpansBuffer.__init__` and stored on `self`, but never read after this change. It also appears in no test or call site (factory.py constructs SpansBuffer without it). Either remove it or wire it back in as a safety net alongside the Lua eviction.

findings.title: organization_context.member may be None for superusers
findings.body: `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` evaluates the right-hand side unconditionally. `organization_context.member` is typed as `RpcOrganizationMember | None`; a superuser who is not a member of this organization (which is exactly the case where the first disjunct is what protects the call) will hit AttributeError on `None.has_global_access`. Use short-circuit-friendly access: `organization_context.member.has_global_access if organization_context.member else False`.

findings.title: No test for new eviction / ZSET path
findings.body:
The behavioural change in this PR — switching from sets to sorted sets, evicting oldest spans above 1000, and tracking `end_timestamp_precise` as score — has zero test coverage. There is no test that:
  - feeds more than 1000 spans into one segment and verifies the resulting cardinality is bounded,
  - verifies that the evicted members are the ones with the lowest score (and therefore that this is observable as data loss),
  - verifies ZUNIONSTORE merge ordering preserves spans by end_timestamp.
Add an explicit regression test before merging; otherwise the eviction rule can change silently.

findings.title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or negative-offset branch
findings.body:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (a new class) and the new `enable_advanced_features` flag have no test coverage. The audit-logs endpoint change that wires it in (superuser OR has_global_access) is similarly untested. Add at least:
  - tests that the new paginator is selected for the documented inputs,
  - tests for the negative-offset code path (and document the expected 500 if/until the Django-slice bug is fixed).
Currently the only signal these paths work is manual QA.

findings.title: Misleading comment about Django ORM negative slicing
findings.body: Comment claims: "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions". This is incorrect: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for any negative slice start. The comment should be removed and the code actually fixed (or replaced with reverse-window logic using `reversed(queryset)` / LIMIT + OFFSET + explicit ordering).
